# Baruch Chapter 6 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal Equivalence)
## [The Letter of Jeremiah]

**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Baruch 6 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/BAR_006_page_001.jpg

---

**1** A copy of the letter that Jeremiah sent to those who were about to be led captive to Babylon by the king of the Babylonians, to tell them what God had commanded him.

**2** Because of the sins that you have committed before God, you will be led away as captives to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians.

**3** When you arrive in Babylon you will remain there for many years, for a long time — up to seven generations; after that I will bring you out from there in peace.

**4** And now in Babylon you will see gods made of silver and gold and wood, carried on people's shoulders, filling the nations with awe.

**5** Beware, therefore, of becoming like those foreigners; do not let fear of them seize you

**6** when you see the crowds before and behind them, worshipping them. But say in your heart: It is you, O Lord, who must be worshipped.

**7** For my angel is with you, and he is watching over your souls.

**8** Their tongues have been polished smooth by a craftsman; they themselves are overlaid with gold and silver; but they are false and cannot speak.

**9** And people bring gold as an offering to them as they would to a girl who loves jewelry —

**10** but the priests take the gold and silver from their gods and spend it on themselves.

**11** They even give some of it to prostitutes on the temple rooftop, and they clothe these wooden, silvered, and gilded gods with garments like human beings.

**12** Yet these gods cannot save themselves from rust and moths, though they are wrapped in purple clothing.

**13** Their faces are wiped because of the thick dust of the temple that settles upon them.

**14** He who cannot put to death anyone who wrongs him wields a scepter like a judge over a country;

**15** he has a dagger in his right hand and an axe; yet he cannot deliver himself from war and brigands.

**16** From this it is evident that they are not gods; so do not fear them.

**17** For just as a man's vessel is made useless when it is broken, so are their gods: when they have been set up in temples, their eyes are filled with dust raised by the feet of those who come in.

**18** And just as all the gates are locked on every side against anyone who has offended a king, condemned to death, so the priests secure their temples with doors, bolts, and bars, in case they are plundered by robbers.

**19** They light more lamps for them than they light for themselves, yet the gods cannot see a single one.

**20** They are like a wooden beam in the house; they say the hearts inside them are eaten out; when creeping things from the ground devour both them and their garments, they feel nothing.

**21** Their faces are blackened by smoke from the temple.

**22** Bats, swallows, and birds perch on their bodies and heads; and so do cats.

**23** From this you will know that they are not gods; so do not fear them.

**24** The gold that beautifies them — unless someone wipes off the tarnish, they will not shine; and even when they were being cast, they had no feeling.

**25** They are purchased without regard to price; there is no breath in them.

**26** Having no feet, they are carried on shoulders; revealing their shame before all mankind; and those who serve them are humiliated as well.

**27** If they are set down on the ground, they cannot rise again; and if anyone tilts one over, it cannot right itself; and offerings placed before them are like offerings placed before the dead.

**28** What is sacrificed to them their priests sell and pocket; and in the same way their wives preserve some of it in brine, but give nothing to the poor or helpless.

**29** Women in menstruation and women in childbirth handle their sacrifices; knowing therefore from these things that they are not gods, do not fear them.

**30** For how can they be called gods? Women serve as officiants at the shrines of these wooden, silvered, and golden gods.

**31** And in their temples the priests sit with torn robes, their heads and beards shaved, and their heads uncovered.

**32** They howl and cry out before their gods the way people wail at a funeral.

**33** The priests take some of their garments and dress their wives and children in them.

**34** Whether you do good or harm to them, they cannot repay it; they can neither set up a king nor depose one.

**35** Likewise, they can neither give wealth nor provide money; if one makes a vow to them and does not keep it, they will not demand an accounting.

**36** They cannot save a person from death or rescue the weak from the powerful.

**37** They cannot restore sight to the blind; they cannot deliver a person in distress.

**38** They cannot show mercy to a widow or do good to an orphan.

**39** Their wooden, gilded, and silvered gods are like the stones of the mountain; those who serve them will be put to shame.

**40** How then can anyone suppose or claim that they are gods?

**41** Even the Chaldeans themselves dishonor them; for when they see a mute person who cannot speak, they bring him and ask Bel to make him speak, as if Bel had understanding.

**42** Yet they themselves cannot perceive this and abandon them; for they have no sense.

**43** The women, wearing cords around them, sit in the streets burning bran as incense; and when one of them is taken aside by a passerby who sleeps with her, she taunts her neighbor who has not been honored as she has, and whose cord has not been cut.

**44** Everything that is done for them is false; how then can anyone suppose or claim that they are gods?

**45** They are made by craftsmen and goldsmiths; they can become nothing other than what those craftsmen intend them to be.

**46** Those who make them cannot themselves live very long; how then can the things they have made be gods?

**47** For they have bequeathed only lies and reproach to those who come after them.

**48** For when war and disaster come upon them, the priests take counsel among themselves about where to hide with the gods.

**49** How then can anyone fail to understand that these are not gods — these things that cannot save themselves from war or calamity?

**50** Since they are made of wood, overlaid with silver and gold, it will be known in due time that they are false; it will become plain to all nations and kings that they are not gods but the work of human hands, and that there is no work of God in them.

**51** Who then can fail to know that they are not gods?

**52** For they cannot set up a king over a land or give rain to human beings.

**53** They cannot adjudicate their own case or deliver one who is wronged; for they are without power; they are like crows between heaven and earth.

**54** When fire breaks out in the house of wooden, silvered, and gilded gods, their priests will flee and escape, while they themselves are burned there like timbers.

**55** Moreover, they cannot withstand a king or enemies; how then can one accept or even think that they are gods?

**56** Gods made of wood, overlaid with silver and gold, are unable to protect themselves from thieves or robbers.

**57** Anyone stronger than they will strip them of their gold and silver and the garments they wear, and go off with it; they will be powerless to help themselves.

**58** Therefore it is better to be a king showing his valor, or a household vessel of service to its master, than to be these false gods; better also a door of a house that keeps safe what is inside, than these false gods; better likewise a wooden pillar of a palace, than these false gods.

**59** For sun and moon and stars are brilliant, and when sent on their errands they are obedient.

**60** Likewise lightning, when it flashes, is a magnificent sight; and the wind blows over every land.

**61** When God commands the clouds to traverse the whole earth, they carry out his order.

**62** And fire, sent from above to consume mountains and forests, does what it has been told. But these gods are not to be compared to any of these, either in appearance or in power.

**63** Therefore one must not think or claim that they are gods; they are unable to give judgment or benefit human beings.

**64** Knowing then that they are not gods, do not fear them.

**65** They can neither curse kings nor bless them.

**66** They show no signs in the sky for the nations, they neither shine like the sun nor give light like the moon.

**67** The wild animals are better off than they are, for they can flee to shelter and look after themselves.

**68** So it is in no way clear to us that they are gods; therefore do not fear them.

**69** For like a scarecrow in a cucumber patch that guards nothing, so are their wooden, silvered, and gilded gods.

**70** In the same way their wooden, gilded, and silvered gods are like a white thornbush in a garden, on which every bird perches; or like a corpse thrown out into the dark.

**71** By the purple and linen cloth that rot upon them you will recognize that they are not gods; and they will finally be consumed themselves and become a reproach in the land.

**72** Better therefore is an upright person who has no idols — for he will be far from reproach.

---
*LOGOS notes: The Letter of Jeremiah is a sustained satirical polemic in the tradition of Jer 10:1-16, Isa 44:9-20, and Ps 115:4-8. The structural refrain appears in varied forms: vv.16, 23, 29, 40, 44, 49, 51, 64, 68, 72 (approximately). The target of the satire is the Babylonian cult, particularly the cult of Bel/Marduk (named explicitly in v.41). The letter was likely composed in Hebrew or Aramaic in the 3rd-2nd century BCE and translated into Greek; the Greek alone survives.*
